title: Graham W. Buhrman
text:
I am a quantitative methodologist and PhD student at the University of Wisconsin–Madison. My research bridges causal machine learning, multilevel modeling, and statistical decision theory to improve educational research and program evaluation. I develop and study methods that help applied researchers accurately identify heterogeneous treatment effects and conduct rigorous and cost-aware program evaluations.

title: About Me
text:
My Background: I am formally trained in quantitative methods within Educational Psychology, with a technical focus on causal inference, multilevel data structures, and nonparametric regression trees. My workflow uses statistical programming in R and high-throughput computing environments.
My Research: My dissertation proposes the ‘Discover, Characterize, Confirm’ (DCC) framework, a methodological pipeline designed to translate complex machine learning algorithms into epistemologically aware and visually interpretable analyses of heterogeneous treatment effects. I have presented my work on the analysis of heterogeneous treatment effects and multilevel analysis at international conferences, including AERA and IMPS, and have published work in the proceedings of IMPS and applied journals.
My Focus: I am dedicated to leveraging the power of causal machine learning to understand and explain the mechanisms of treatment effect variation across populations in education research. By building accessible methodological workflows, I aim to prevent evaluations from masking heterogeneity while mitigating the false interpretations of spurious patterns as treatment variation. Ultimately, my work is in the pursuit of developing and scaling cost-effective interventions and programs in education that bring the maximum possible benefit to people.

title: Interactive Network Demo
text:
The interactive network below maps the conceptual and methodological terrain of my dissertation work. It illustrates how the “Discover, Characterize, Confirm” (DCC) framework bridges the gap between predictive machine learning and econometric causal inference.

Instructions: You can click and drag the nodes to see the physics engine react. Clicking on a specific node will highlight its direct methodological and theoretical connections.


library(visNetwork)

# Define the nodes and assign them to thematic groups for automatic color-coding
nodes <- data.frame(
  id = 1:9, 
  label = c(
    "DCC Framework", 
    "Heterogeneous Treatment Effects", 
    "Bayesian Additive Regression Trees", 
    "Debiased Machine Learning", 
    "Hierarchical Linear Modeling", 
    "Econometrics", 
    "Measurement", 
    "Project STAR", 
    "Cost-Effectiveness"
  ),
  group = c(
    "Core", 
    "Theory", 
    "Methodology", 
    "Methodology", 
    "Methodology", 
    "Theory", 
    "Theory", 
    "Application", 
    "Application"
  ),
  value = c(25, 15, 15, 15, 10, 15, 10, 15, 10) # Makes the central nodes slightly larger
)

# Define the directional edges (connections) between the nodes
edges <- data.frame(
  from = c(1, 1, 1, 1, 2, 3, 6, 6, 7, 7, 8, 2), 
  to   = c(2, 3, 4, 8, 5, 4, 4, 2, 2, 8, 9, 9)
)

# Render the interactive widget
visNetwork(nodes, edges, width = "100%", height = "600px") |>
  visNodes(shape = "dot", shadow = TRUE, font = list(size = 16)) |>
  visEdges(arrows = "to", color = list(opacity = 0.5)) |>
  visOptions(
    highlightNearest = list(enabled = TRUE, degree = 1, hover = TRUE), 
    nodesIdSelection = TRUE
  ) |>
  visPhysics(stabilization = FALSE) |>
  visInteraction(navigationButtons = TRUE) # Adds zoom controls
